doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Joining Willie Bryant's band as a trumpet-playing sideman
summary: After his band broke up he took a job, mainly on trumpet, with Willie Bryant, who was not a musician.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: As your band finally broke up, you . . .
For the umpth time, or the umpteenth time.
[laughs] And was to again years later, but we’ll get into that.
Yes, indeed.
You yourself went from being a leader of your own orchestra playing in many of the leading venues, you went to becoming a sideman again . . .
That’s right.
. . . this time with Willy Bryant.
Oh yes.
Do you remember your feelings at the time? Was this a letdown? Was this just another way of getting . . .
Just another step in some direction, hopefully, the proper direction, and good to have a job.
And what sort of band did Willy Bryant have?
I don’t remember. I really don’t. There are a couple of records available, which I don’t think I’ve ever heard.
I believe you played trumpet, mostly, with [unclear].
Yeah. Well, I didn’t play saxophone at all, I don’t think. In that band, I was just in the trumpet section.
Was that one reason you joined? Did you want to work more as a trumpet player?
Well, it was one reason, but I guess the main reason was that I didn’t have a job. [laughter] We can’t escape that, Ed. We can’t escape that.
Okay.
Yep.
Some of the musicians have implied, if not stated outright, that—I think Ben Webster did—that [when] you joined the band, you became musical director of Willy Bryant’s band. Was that . . .

I may have. It was a very short stint, but Willy Bryant was not a musician. He didn’t play an instrument. He didn’t read music. He sang a little. So there had to be somebody giving him some musical guidance. It might have been me, I don’t know.
But as far as you recall, it wasn’t a formal arrangement [unclear] join.
No, no, indeed not.
